analysis.title: Oil: the calm before another storm?
key_insights: ANZ raises its 31 December Brent forecast from USD95/bbl to USD105/bbl. The revision does not assume another escalation in Middle East hostilities.

The raise reflects physical constraints that ANZ does not expect to dissipate before year-end: Hormuz throughput, tanker availability, depleted refined-product inventories and zero effective surplus OPEC capacity.
The US midterm elections on 3 November are the next geopolitical catalyst. Renewed hostilities after the vote would hit a market with fewer buffers than at the start of the conflict.

Eight months of adapting to disrupted Middle East supply have drawn down strategic inventories, tightened tankers, stretched alternative export routes and depleted refined products. ANZ's Oil Market Resilience Dashboard rates conditions 'vulnerable'.

Persian Gulf exports were 14.3mb/d as of 26 October and weakening. Effective Hormuz throughput is about 60% of the pre-conflict normal. Global distillate stocks are 4.9% below the five-year average and diesel cracks reached USD103.8/bbl.

Productive capacity and deliverable capacity have diverged. Gulf producers may be able to raise output, but extra barrels cannot readily transit Hormuz or move through constrained pipelines and tanker supply.
ANZ argues the marginal cost of disruption is rising: losing the next barrel could move prices more than losing the first, which is the core of the forecast revision.
Shipping is acting as spare capacity. Attacks on tankers rose by mid-October, shuttling out of the Gulf adds about a week to some voyages, and Gulf-to-China VLCC hire costs approached USD1m/day.
Global spare crude inventory cover fell to about 41 days from nearly 45 days earlier this year. Strategic reserves are not exhausted but their marginal effectiveness is diminishing.

Product markets are the pressure point. Distillate inventories are 4.9% below the five-year average and diesel cracks are near USD104/bbl, which supports crude even without new geopolitical deterioration.

Part of the weak 2026 oil demand reflects supply-constrained demand (product shortages, high transport costs, trade restrictions, refining bottlenecks). Better supply would revive some of that demand and slow the return to surplus.

Chinese crude imports recovered to just over 9mb/d in September, with October weekly volumes above 9.5mb/d. Refinery throughput is at a six-month high and domestic crude stocks are being drawn. ANZ sees this as a price floor.
Scenario 1, de-escalation: a credible diplomatic breakthrough plus better shipping could take Brent to USD90-95/bbl. ANZ says this removes the geopolitical premium but not the scarcity premium.
Scenario 2, status quo (base case): Brent around USD105/bbl at year-end with Hormuz below normal, tight tankers, elevated freight and depleted product stocks.
Scenario 3, renewed escalation: a convex price response is possible. ANZ treats USD120/bbl and above as a scenario marker, not a formal forecast.

ANZ lists seven indicators to watch: Hormuz throughput, Persian Gulf exports, tanker rates and availability, war-risk insurance, diesel cracks, Chinese crude imports and inventory cover. Brent rising alongside falling exports, higher freight, wider cracks and stronger backwardation signals physical tightening rather than a risk premium.

sector_views.rationale: ANZ sees risks to its USD105/bbl Brent forecast skewed to the upside because physical constraints persist and buffers are depleted.

macro_indicators.interpretation: ANZ's base case is a status-quo scenario that assumes current physical constraints persist, with no new escalation.
ANZ now views this as closer to a de-escalation outcome than to the current physical market.
Reached only with a credible diplomatic breakthrough and better shipping conditions.
A scenario marker rather than a formal forecast, applying if escalation materially impairs regional exports.
Exports were weakening, which would confirm physical tightening if the decline continues.
Limits how many additional barrels can reach the market.

macro_indicators.indicator: Global distillate inventories vs five-year average
macro_indicators.interpretation: Product tightness supports crude prices and would amplify any new disruption.
A further surge alongside falling inventories would signal stress passing through refining to consumers.
Down from about 45 days earlier this year, so less insurance against another shock.

macro_indicators.reading: just over 9mb/d in September, weekly above 9.5mb/d in October
macro_indicators.interpretation: Recovering Chinese buying acts as a floor under prices.
ANZ's estimate under prevailing logistical constraints. Immediately deliverable spare capacity is limited.

risk_factors: Renewed escalation in Hormuz traffic, damage to export infrastructure or attacks that deter tankers would hit a market with little flexibility and could push Brent above USD120/bbl.
Depleted strategic and commercial inventories, with cover near 41 days.
Constrained tanker capacity and VLCC hire costs near USD1m/day.
Depleted refined-product inventories and diesel cracks near USD104/bbl.
Downside risk if a diplomatic breakthrough unwinds the geopolitical premium, towards USD90-95/bbl, though Chinese buying and demand recovery would limit the fall.
vol_and_positioning: ANZ says geopolitical premiums and positioning can adjust faster than physical fundamentals, so a credible de-escalation could trigger a sharp correction in Brent.
Freight rates, physical differentials and backwardation would probably weaken alongside Brent in a de-escalation.
Brent rising with stronger backwardation, higher freight and wider cracks would signal physical tightening rather than a risk premium.
geopolitical: Middle East hostilities escalated in February and have disrupted Persian Gulf supply for eight months.
US midterm elections on 3 November are seen as the next catalyst, with a possibility of renewed hostilities after the vote.
Attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz increased substantially by mid-October.
Planned G7 strategic reserve releases provided relief to stressed product markets.
A credible diplomatic breakthrough on Hormuz transits is the main de-escalation path.

tension_points.bull_case: Physical constraints persist: Hormuz at about 60% of normal, zero effective OPEC spare capacity, inventory cover near 41 days and diesel cracks near USD104/bbl support USD105/bbl, with USD120/bbl-plus on escalation.
tension_points.bear_case: A credible diplomatic breakthrough with better shipping could unwind the geopolitical premium and take Brent towards USD90-95/bbl, though Chinese buying and demand recovery would limit the fall.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Brent rising on headlines alone is only a risk premium. Falling Persian Gulf exports, higher freight, wider diesel cracks and stronger backwardation would confirm physical tightening and threaten the forecast on the upside.

theme_stances.key_argument: Buffers are depleted, so the next barrel lost would have a larger price impact than the first.
theme_stances.evidence: The market has adapted. It has not recovered.

theme_stances.key_argument: Throughput near 60% of normal, tight tankers and depleted product stocks keep the market short of flexibility.
theme_stances.evidence: Shipping capacity has consequently become another form of global spare capacity.

theme_stances.key_argument: A fall in crude prices would prompt Chinese refiners to accelerate purchases and rebuild stocks.
theme_stances.evidence: This provides an important floor beneath the price's downside potential.
